L:text.html.markdown.mdy - meta.embedded.comment: THE load-bearing rule. The markdown grammar claims headings, list items, emphasis, tables, quotes, fences… as its own begin/end contexts, and inside those contexts the top-level patterns below are never consulted — without this injection, `# {{ title }}` and `- {{ x }}` lose their tag delimiters entirely (the shipped 0.0.1 bug). `L:` injects these with priority at every position of every markdown context; the exclusions keep it from re-matching inside an already-open tag or inside front matter (where {{ }} is literal YAML, never templated). #document-separator is here for the same reason: after a paragraph line, markdown reads `body` + `---` as a setext heading and consumes the --- INSIDE its paragraph context, but splitDocuments splits on a bare --- unconditionally, wherever it appears. Known divergence, accepted: a tag inside an inline `code span` stays unhighlighted — the span's match starts at the earlier backtick and leftmost-wins beats injection priority — even though the engine does run tags there.

frontmatter-start.comment: YAML front matter at the very start of the file. A TextMate grammar tokenizes one line at a time, so a begin pattern can never look ahead to confirm a later line is a bare +++ (the real, only rule src/mdy.js uses — see FRONT_MATTER_SEPARATOR/parseDocument). This approximates it from the one line we CAN see: front matter starts where the first line looks like a YAML `key:` mapping entry, or is +++ itself (an empty front-matter block, which parseDocument explicitly allows). A document whose body happens to open with `Word: text` is the one (rare, and not seen anywhere in this repo's own examples) case this over-triggers on.
frontmatter-start.name: meta.frontmatter.mdy

document-separator.comment: A bare --- line splits a source into multiple documents (splitDocuments). Each new document may have its own front matter, checked the same heuristic way as frontmatter-start, against the line immediately following the separator; otherwise this --- is just a plain separator and what follows is body. `end` is a zero-width lookahead for any real (non-newline) character, deliberately NOT [\s\S]: vscode-textmate appends a synthetic trailing newline to every tokenized line (so $ anchors work), and [\s\S] would match THAT, closing this region one line too early — before the nested front-matter pattern below ever gets a look at the real next line. The separator carries markup.heading.* IN ADDITION to its punctuation scope (space-separated names push both onto the token's scope stack, deeper one last): a bare --- is the file's most structural line — it starts a whole new document — and plain punctuation scopes render dim in most themes. markup.heading is the scope family themes reliably make bold/colored, and 'a new document starts here' is exactly a heading-weight event. Same treatment for the +++ front-matter fences.
document-separator.name: meta.after-document-separator.mdy

escape.comment: \{{ and \{% render as literal {{ / {% (compileTemplateSource's emitLiteral unescape) — never tag delimiters. Listed before the tag rules everywhere (root and injection); at the same position isn't even needed — the escape's match starts at the backslash, one column earlier than the brace, and leftmost always wins.
escape.name: constant.character.escape.mdy

tag-output.comment: {{ expr }} — an output tag; expr is a JS expression whose value is stringified into the rendered markdown. Closes at the FIRST }}, matching the engine (compileTemplateSource uses indexOf, not brace counting). contentName, NOT name: meta.embedded.line.mdy is mapped to JavaScript in package.json's embeddedLanguages, and a region's `name` covers its begin/end delimiters too — which made VSCode treat the {{ }} braces themselves as JS-language brackets and rainbow-colorize them as nested pairs. With contentName only the expr between the delimiters is JS; the delimiters stay mdy-language punctuation, governed by mdy's own language configuration (which disables bracket-pair colorization).
tag-output.name: meta.template.expression.mdy

tag-code.comment: {% ... %} — a code tag; contents are raw JS statements (control flow, declarations, $.emit/$.render calls) spliced directly into the compiled template function. Braces need not balance within a single tag (a { for/if } is often opened in one tag and closed in a later one) — which is exactly why these patterns must NOT include the real source.js grammar: its brace-block begin/end regions would open on the unbalanced { and swallow the %} (a region's end pattern is only consulted while it is top-of-stack). The #js-* rules below are deliberately region-free (or closer-guarded) so the tag's own end pattern always stays live, and the tag closes at the FIRST %}, exactly like the engine's indexOf. contentName, not name — see tag-output's comment.
tag-code.name: meta.template.statement.mdy

js-in-statement-tag.comment: JS highlighting inside {% %}. Strings and comments are guarded against %} — the engine closes the tag at the first %} even inside a string or comment (indexOf knows no JS), so a construct that spanned the closer would both diverge from the engine and eat the delimiter. Guarded constructs simply stop highlighting at the closer; the plain text that remains is a smaller loss than a swallowed tag.

js-in-expression-tag.comment: Same as #js-in-statement-tag with }} as the guarded closer. (%} needs no guard here — it's plain content inside an output tag, and vice versa.)

js-common.comment: Region-free JS token rules shared by both tag types. Every rule here is a single match that cannot span a closer (single-char operator matches can start AT a closer's first char, but a region's end pattern is checked before inner patterns at the same position, so the closer still wins). $ before . is the template's native-function namespace ($.find, $.render, $.emit, $.resize, …) — highlighted like a language-provided variable, not a plain identifier.
